Association tests (habitat × pathway): chi-square = 75.20, df=18, p = 5.8e-09 (caveat: small cells); 20,000-permutation test (robust) p < 5e-05. Pathway composition clearly varies by habitat.

========================================================================

Riparian              2.196    0.257      (1.328,3.631)  yes
Rock outcrops         ~0      (separation, infinite CI)  n/a
Scrublands            1.929    0.600      (0.595,6.256)  no
Urban                 1.959    0.257      (1.184,3.242)  yes
Wetlands              3.683    0.274      (2.154,6.297)  yes
All 6 environmental covariates: OR ≈ 0.99–1.33, all 95% CIs include 1 (none significant).

KEY QUESTION — does the habitat effect remain significant after adding covariates?
• Individual habitat contrasts: YES for the well-sampled water-associated + urban habitats — Wetlands (OR 3.68), Coastal (3.92), Riparian (2.20), Urban (1.96) all keep 95% CIs excluding 1 after adjustment.
• Overall habitat block: BORDERLINE. LRT (Model B vs env-only) chi2=14.65, df=9, p=0.10 (not sig at 0.05); Wald test W=28.60, df=9, p=0.0008 (sig). The LRT/Wald split is driven by under-dispersion (φ≈0.45) + separation in the tiny habitats.
• Environment adds NO independent power: LRT (Model B vs habitat-only) p=0.65.
→ Interpretation: habitat and environment are strongly collinear (habitat is essentially a proxy for elevation/water/urbanization). The gardening gradient is real and persists for the key habitats, but "habitat type per se" vs "environment" cannot be cleanly separated — it is a joint habitat–environment gradient.

SENSITIVITY (Model B excluding the two separation habitats, n=187): key ORs essentially unchanged — Wetlands 3.71 (2.16,6.37), Coastal 3.96 (2.10,7.48), Riparian 2.21 (1.33,3.66), Urban 1.97 (1.19,3.27). Conclusions are robust.

========================================================================
PROPOSED FINAL HYPOTHESIS (anchored on gardening share; robust to other readings)
========================================================================
"Gardening is the single most important introduction pathway for non-native plants in the Barcelona study area, and its prevalence is strongly habitat-dependent, tracking a habitat–environment gradient. Gardening-introduced species make up a much larger share of the non-native flora in water-associated, low-elevation habitats — wetlands (≈0.56), coastal (≈0.54) and riparian (≈0.37) — and, to a lesser degree, urban (≈0.30) habitats, than in agricultural croplands (≈0.19) or rock-outcrop habitats (≈0). Among well-sampled habitats the gradient runs wetlands/coastal (highest) → riparian/urban (intermediate) → croplands (lowest). The pattern is statistically robust (habitat × pathway χ² = 75.2, p < 1e-8; permutation p < 5e-5) and persists after adjusting for elevation, urban/cropland cover and distance to roads/streams (adjusted odds of a gardening introduction 2.2–3.7× higher in wetlands, coastal, riparian and urban than croplands; all 95% CIs exclude 1). Because habitat and these environmental covariates are strongly collinear (environment adds no independent power, p = 0.65), the pattern is best read as a habitat–environment gradient — gardening introductions concentrate where water, low elevation and human modification coincide — rather than an effect of habitat label in isolation."

Supporting evidence (robustness to 'prevalence'):
• Absolute count (mean n.gard/plot): highest Coastal 0.79, Wetlands 0.76, Urban 0.69; lowest Croplands 0.22, forests/rock ≈0.
• Probability a plot has ≥1 gardening species: highest Wetlands 50%, Urban 48%, Coastal 45%; lowest Rock outcrops 0%, Scrublands 2%.
• Species-level corroboration (invasion_success_pathways.csv): 42/81 records (54.5% of 77 unique species) are gardening-introduced; gardening species occupy slightly fewer habitat types on average (1.95 vs 2.21 overall).

WORKFLOW (for the submission):
1. Loaded plot-level invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots × 37 vars; one row/plot; n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo = n.total on every row).
2. Step 1: per-habitat gardening share + Wilson 95% CI, mean n.gard/plot, % plots with ≥1 gardening species; flagged <10-invaded-species habitats; tested habitat × pathway via χ² and a 20,000-permutation test.
3. Step 2: quasibinomial GLM (binomial + Pearson-dispersion correction; trials = n.total) of gardening share ~ habitat on the 191 invaded plots, then + z-standardized environmental covariates; compared by LRT and Wald; sensitivity fit excluding separation habitats.
4. Supporting context: the region-wide temporal contingency table shows gardening rising 18 → 54 → 142 → 397 species across the four periods (85% of 1985–2019 introductions) — i.e., a dynamic, now-dominant pathway, not a static one.
5. The two CSVs share no species/plot key, so the habitat question was answered from the plot-level file; the species-level file was used only as corroboration.

ARTIFACTS SAVED in /workspace:
• analysis.py (executed script)
• step1_habitat_gardening_summary.csv (Step-1 table)
• step2_glm_habitat_only.csv, step2_glm_habitat_plus_covariates.csv
• analysis_results.md (full numeric output)

LIMITATIONS / UNCERTAINTIES:
• Four habitats have <10 invaded species (Rock outcrops 1, Broad-leaved 4, Scrublands 5, Coniferous 8); their point estimates (e.g., Broad-leaved 1.00, Coniferous 0.88) are unreliable and flagged — do not over-interpret the forest categories.
• The GLM is under-dispersed (φ≈0.45) with separation in the tiny habitats, so the overall habitat-block test is borderline (LRT p≈0.08–0.10; Wald p≈0.0005–0.0008); the individual well-sampled contrasts are stable and significant in both, and unchanged in the sensitivity fit.
• Habitat and environment are strongly collinear → the pattern is a joint habitat–environment gradient, not a cleanly separable habitat effect.
• 441/632 uninvaded plots (n.total=0) carry no pathway info and are excluded from the share metric.
• n.gard is a per-plot species count; 'prevalence' is reported three ways (share, mean count, plot probability) to be robust to interpretation.

Please confirm the hypothesis wording and the Step-1/Step-2 presentation, and I will finalize the submission (answer = hypothesis; payload.hypothesis + payload.workflow; artifacts = analysis.py + step1 table).
